results.summary: Tappu is an 8-bit CPU inspired by the esoteric language BF, implemented in Chisel. It includes a ROM that causes all outputs to blink, and the design is intended to be observed by watching the output blink. The documentation is minimal, providing only a brief description and no detailed usage or testing instructions. No external hardware is required beyond power and observation of the outputs.

This module captures timestamps of rising edges on input triggers, referenced to an internal 24-bit counter with a period of about 30 ms. It provides a data-ready signal and allows reading the captured timestamp via a clocked serial interface. The design is intended for capturing events and may benefit from a signal generator for testing. The documentation notes that it was tested manually only once in simulation, indicating limited verification.

This design displays a bouncing Tiny Tapeout logo on a VGA screen at 640x480 resolution, with options for tiling and solid color. It can be controlled with an optional gamepad to pause, change direction, or move the logo. The design requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and optionally a Gamepad Pmod for interaction. Silicon testing confirmed it works, showing the bouncing logo as intended.

Sequential Shadows Deluxe is a demo competition entry for TT08 that generates VGA video and audio, featuring visual effects and music. It requires a TinVGA or Pmod VGA for video output and Mike's audio Pmod for sound, with pinout selection via an input. The demo includes flashing lights by default, which can be disabled via inputs. The design is notable for its integration of video and audio in a single submission.

Orion Iron Ion is a TT10 demo competition entry that produces VGA video and audio, including a logo, star field, floating-point unit for graphics, and a synthesizer. It requires a TinyVGA Pmod and Mike's audio Pmod for full functionality. The demo starts automatically after reset and was verified working on silicon by the author. The design is notable for its use of a floating-point unit in a demo context.

Cgates tests two different implementations of Muller's C-gate: one using a latch and one using combinatorial logic, and also builds rings of various lengths from these gates. The design allows observation of the C-gate outputs and ring oscillations, with testing requiring an oscilloscope for the ring outputs. It is a variant of a previous design and serves as an experiment in asynchronous logic elements. The documentation provides clear instructions for basic testing.

toni_clk_gen generates multiple clock signals by dividing the input frequency. It provides two divided clock outputs, but the documentation does not specify the division ratios or intended application. The testing procedure is unknown, and external hardware such as a clock generator is suggested. The design appears to be a simple clock divider experiment with minimal documentation.

This design implements an asynchronous locking unit that accepts eight request signals and provides eight grant signals, ensuring that only one grant is active at a time. It functions as a mutual exclusion arbiter for asynchronous systems. The documentation is brief and does not describe the arbitration policy or testing methodology. No external hardware is specified.

Wirecube is a demo for the Tiny Tapeout demoscene competition that displays a rotating wireframe cube on a VGA screen. It requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and operates at a clock frequency of 50.35 MHz. Inputs allow toggling background and cube colors, as well as speed. The documentation is sparse and will be updated after the competition, but the design is functional as a visual demo.

This design implements a 4x4 array multiplier using structural logic, taking two 4-bit inputs and producing an 8-bit product. It uses full adders to sum partial products along diagonals. The design is purely combinational and requires no external hardware. The documentation includes diagrams and a GitHub link, but the testing procedure is simply to apply inputs and observe the output.
